# Harrowgate Community Trust

## Six-month programme plan: January–June 2026

**Programming budget:** £60,000  
**Period:** 1 January – 30 June 2026  
**Prepared for:** the Board of Trustees

> The £60,000 covers programming only. The east hall repair is a separate capital grant application, and the family fund is separate and capped at £9,000. Neither is included in the £60,000.

---

## 1. The plan in brief

The trust's attendance decline is not confined to evenings. Tuesday craft fell 14% and Thursday film fell 22% in 2025. Saturday family rose 21% year-on-year, but that rise is a step-change from introducing childcare, not continuing growth: once both years had childcare (September–December), family attendance was flat (40.0 in 2024 against 39.2 in 2025). Transport may be part of the story, but it cannot explain the fall in morning sessions. The plan therefore keeps the core programme running as a control and adds four bounded pieces of new work, each aimed at a different explanation for the decline.

| Strand | What happens | Explanation tested |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Core programme (control)** | Tuesday craft, Thursday film and Saturday family workshop continue | Is the decline general, or specific to one session? |
| **Family and childcare** | Weekly Saturday workshop with free childcare, funded by the family fund | Caring responsibilities; family demand |
| **Friday Nights** | Eight evening events with a hired minibus, free entry and measured attendance | Transport; evening demand |
| **Sunday Sessions** | Six low-cost afternoon sessions | Changed habits and time preference; there is no local evidence |
| **East hall** | A spring exhibition and a May–June community season, gated on HVAC commissioning | Programming quality and scale; better use of the building |

Two gates keep the board in control: **20 February** (east hall) and **24 April** (Friday Nights). A final evaluation on **30 June** recommends what should continue.

---

## 2. Month-by-month schedule

### January 2026 — baseline and first tests

- **Core:** Tuesday craft group on 6, 13, 20 and 27 January, 10:00–12:00, workshop room. Thursday film club on 8, 15, 22 and 29 January, 19:00–21:00, west hall. Saturday family workshop on 3, 10, 17, 24 and 31 January, 10:00–12:00, west hall, with free childcare 10:00–14:00 from the family fund.
- **Friday Nights:** #1 on Friday 16 January and #2 on Friday 30 January, 19:00–21:30, west hall and café. Minibus from the market square at 18:15, returning at 21:45. Free entry, donations. #1 is a local history talk; #2 is a film and discussion.
- **Sunday Sessions:** #1 on Sunday 25 January, 14:00–16:00, west hall: a winter talk and simple making session.
- **Evidence:** by Friday 9 January, compile the 2025 monthly baseline; brief staff and volunteers on counting, postcodes and transport mode; open booking for January and February. The booking sheet records seats reserved, seats taken, minibus passengers and how people got home.
- **East hall:** no activity. Confirm in writing with the building officer and the council the grant approval, repair date and commissioning test. Do not book the hall until commissioning is confirmed.
- **Marketing:** launch the season; £600 on local print, social media and targeted distribution to the four estates and family networks.

### February 2026 — confirm the east hall; keep the tests running

- **Core:** craft on 3, 10 and 24 February (no session on 17 February, half-term); film on 5, 12, 19 and 26 February; family workshop on 7, 14, 21 and 28 February with childcare.
- **Friday Nights:** #3 on Friday 13 February (music and spoken word) and #4 on Friday 27 February (film and discussion), with the minibus.
- **Sunday Sessions:** #2 on Sunday 22 February, 14:00–16:00.
- **East hall gate — Friday 20 February:** if commissioning is confirmed for 1 March, release the spring exhibition installation (9–13 March) and opening (14 March). If commissioning is not confirmed, move the exhibition to the west hall and workshop room at reduced scale, keep the dates, and use the contingency for temporary display. No sensitive material is stored in the east hall or the basement in either case.
- **Marketing:** spring exhibition call-out to local makers and community groups; half-term family promotion.

### March 2026 — the east hall opens

- **Core:** craft on 3, 10, 17, 24 and 31 March; film on 5, 12, 19 and 26 March; family workshop on 7, 14, 21 and 28 March with childcare.
- **East hall:** install Monday 9–Friday 13 March. “Made in Harrowgate” opens on Saturday 14 March, 18:00–20:00, and runs to Sunday 12 April. Eight artist-led workshops run at weekends, in the workshop room and east hall. The opening event has two staff.
- **Friday Nights:** #5 on Friday 13 March and #6 on Friday 27 March, with the minibus.
- **Sunday Sessions:** #3 on Sunday 22 March.
- **Marketing:** exhibition and Easter campaign.
- **If the gate failed:** the exhibition is in the west hall at 60 capacity, the workshop programme is capped accordingly, and the opening event moves to the café.

### April 2026 — Easter, and the Friday decision

- **Core:** craft on 7, 14, 21 and 28 April; film on 9, 23 and 30 April (fortnightly, plus an extra screening); family workshop on 4, 11, 18 and 25 April with childcare.
- **Easter family day:** Saturday 4 April, 10:00–14:00, east hall (or west hall if the gate failed). Two artist-led sessions, materials for 80 participants, café open. It combines with the regular Saturday workshop, so the usual childcare applies.
- **Spring exhibition:** closes Sunday 12 April.
- **Friday Nights:** #7 on Friday 10 April and #8 on Friday 24 April, with the minibus.
- **Sunday Sessions:** #4 on Sunday 19 April.
- **Friday gate — Friday 24 April:** review the eight events against the 2023 pilot: average attendance, booking-to-attendance conversion, minibus passengers, postcodes, and whether people say they would return. If the thresholds are met, release #9 (15 May) and #10 (12 June). If not, cancel them and return the £1,500 to the board.
- **Marketing:** Easter and May campaign.

### May 2026 — second east hall season

- **Core:** craft on 5, 12 and 19 May (no session on 26 May, half-term); film on 7 and 21 May; family workshop on 2, 9, 16, 23 and 30 May with childcare.
- **East hall:** “Harrowgate Open” community season installs 18–22 May, opens Saturday 23 May and runs to Sunday 21 June. Six workshops with schools and community groups; family-friendly.
- **Friday Nights:** #9 on Friday 15 May, only if the April gate was met.
- **Sunday Sessions:** #5 on Sunday 17 May.
- **Budget review:** mid-May, compare actuals with the budget and confirm the contingency position before the summer showcase.
- **Marketing:** bank holiday and half-term campaign.

### June 2026 — summer showcase and evaluation

- **Core:** craft on 2, 9, 16, 23 and 30 June; film on 4, 18 and 25 June; family workshop on 6, 13, 20 and 27 June with childcare.
- **East hall:** the season continues. **Summer Showcase** on Saturday 20 June, 12:00–20:00, east hall and café: performances, a makers' market and family activities. Two staff after 18:00; building empty by 21:00.
- **Friday Nights:** #10 on Friday 12 June, only if the gate was met.
- **Sunday Sessions:** #6 on Sunday 14 June.
- **Evaluation:** 22–30 June. Compile attendance, reach, revenue, membership and cost per attendance by strand; report to the board on 30 June with a recommendation for autumn/winter.
- **Marketing:** summer showcase and membership campaign.

---

## 3. Budget

All figures use the rates in `spaces-and-costs.md`, gross. The budget assumes 24 craft sessions, 20 film screenings and 26 family workshops. Materials assume 10 craft participants and 12 family participants per session; buy to the actual register.

### Budget notes

- The east hall repair (£18,000) is a capital grant application and is not in this budget.
- Childcare is not in this budget; it is a draw on the separate family fund (see below).
- No earned income is assumed. The pack gives no ticket prices, so ticket, donation and café income will be recorded separately rather than forecast.
- The £1,500 Friday extension is released only if the 24 April gate is met. If it is not, the programme total is £58,500 and the balance returns to the board.
- Contingency covers repair delay and west hall fallback, artist replacement, extra minibus runs and accessibility costs. It is released by the director with the board chair's agreement.

### Family fund memo (outside the £60,000)

| Item | Basis | £ |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Saturday childcare, weekly | 26 × £180 | 4,680 |
| Family fund cap | | 9,000 |
| Remaining if weekly childcare is approved | | 4,320 |

The cap does not prevent weekly childcare: 26 Saturdays at £180 is £4,680, just over half of the £9,000. The real constraint is that the trustees have not committed the fund. The plan asks for a decision at the board's January meeting so that families can be told. If the trustees approve only fortnightly childcare (13 × £180 = £2,340), the Saturday workshop still runs every week; only the childcare is reduced. The £60,000 programme does not backfill childcare without a separate board decision.

---

## 4. Rationale: evidence and uncertainty

### 4.1 What I relied on

The attendance record (`attendance-2024-2025.csv`) is the strongest evidence because it records behaviour rather than opinion. Comparing 2025 with 2024:

- Tuesday craft: average 33.9 → 29.2 (−14%).
- Thursday film: 20.7 → 16.2 (−22%).
- Saturday family: 31.2 → 37.8 (+21%), but the gain is concentrated in January–August 2025, when 2024 had no childcare. In September–December, when both years had childcare, the averages are 40.0 (2024) and 39.2 (2025). The family session has the strongest attendance level, but it is not on a continuing growth curve.

The decline is therefore broad-based across the core programme: craft and film are down, and the family gain is a step-up that has flattened. That matters. Transport may depress evening attendance, but it cannot by itself explain the fall in Tuesday-morning craft or Saturday-morning family workshops. The plan does not treat transport as the single cause.

The 2025 member survey (`member-survey-2025.md`) puts transport first (61%), but the volunteer's method note is explicit that the evening-transport question was hypothetical: “we asked people to imagine a bus”, with no price test and no behaviour test. 35% said they would not attend even with transport. I treat the survey as a reason to test transport, not as proof of demand. Childcare is cited by 27%, and 81% of those are members with children under 12; that is consistent with the family strand, but it is still a stated preference.

The staff interviews (`staff-interviews.md`) provide two useful facts and one opinion. The facts: the 2023 pilot had no minibus because driver funding fell through, and attendance fell 37 → 23 → 19 while bookings fell 60 → 48. The opinion: “people liked the films; the problem was getting home.” The opinion is plausible, but the pilot is not a clean test of evening demand. It never offered transport, and the first-night booking-to-attendance conversion was only 62%, so something else may also have been happening. The right response is a small, instrumented retest with transport, not a permanent ban or a full-scale commitment.

The prior interventions (`prior-interventions.md`) support a portfolio rather than a single bet. The 2024 childcare pilot is the best positive signal (average 27 → 42), but it is a before/after comparison confounded by seasonality, novelty and the fact that 2024 was already a declining year. The 2022 outreach van had no written evaluation. The 2024 website migration raised traffic 12% but did not change attendance, which suggests that marketing and website work alone will not reverse the decline. The 2023 film pilot is a negative signal about evening events without transport, not a verdict on evening events with transport.

The building and money facts (`constraints.md`, `spaces-and-costs.md`) set the boundaries. The east hall HVAC failed in January 2025; the £18,000 repair is a separate capital grant, expected in late February 2026 and usable from 1 March only if approved and commissioned. The 2019 “climate-controlled” description is stale and is not relied on. The family fund is separate and capped at £9,000; 26 Saturdays × £180 = £4,680, so weekly childcare fits the cap with £4,320 to spare. The binding constraint is trustee discretion, not the cap, so the plan asks for a decision but does not make the family workshop depend on it.

### 4.2 Earlier notes I have corrected

| Earlier note | How I treat it |
| --- | --- |
| “East hall is climate-controlled” (2019 survey, carried forward) | Not relied on. The HVAC failed in January 2025; the hall is used only after written commissioning. |
| “2023 evening pilot failed” | A negative signal, not a settled verdict. The pilot had no transport; bookings were 60 and 48 against attendance of 37, 23 and 19. |
| “Members want evening events” | An overread of a stated preference. 44% said yes, 21% maybe and 35% no; the method note says the question was hypothetical. |
| “Saturday childcare raised attendance” | Promising but not proven. The 27 → 42 step-up is real, but the 2025 gain flattens once both years have childcare. |

The 2023 note's own condition — do not repeat an evening series without transport — is met: every Friday Night has a minibus and two staff. That is the difference between repeating the pilot and testing the question it left open.

### 4.3 What I am uncertain about

- **The cause of the decline.** It is probably multiple. The plan is designed to discriminate between explanations, not to prove one. If the Friday pilot succeeds and Sunday fails, transport and evening access look more important. If both fail while the east hall exhibition draws new people, programming and scale look more important. If everything stays flat, changed habits are the better explanation.
- **Whether transport is the binding constraint.** The survey is stated preference, and the 2023 pilot lacked transport. The Friday test gives a behavioural answer, but eight events is a small sample and winter weather may depress turnout.
- **Whether childcare is causal.** The step-up could be a one-off level shift, seasonality or novelty. The plan continues it because it is affordable and consistent with the evidence, but it measures unique families and repeat attendance rather than assuming the effect.
- **East hall timing.** The repair and commissioning are outside the trust's control. The 20 February gate and the west hall fallback protect the programme, but if commissioning slips beyond June, the board's east hall requirement cannot be met in this period.
- **Sunday demand.** There is no local evidence, and the survey ranks Sunday afternoon last (12%). The pilot is deliberately small; it is a probe, not a core bet.
- **The attendance unit in the CSV.** The file does not say whether the figures are monthly totals or per-session averages. The materials assumptions use 10–12 participants per session and should be checked against the register. If the figures are per-session, materials will cost more and the contingency or the board will need to adjust.
- **Income.** The pack contains no ticket price or earned-income data, so the plan does not assume income. Revenue will be tracked, not targeted.
- **Staff capacity.** The plan budgets bought-in evening cover, but 20 film nights plus 10 Friday Nights is a heavy evening roster. If cover cannot be recruited, the film club should move to fortnightly and the savings held.

### 4.4 How success will be judged

A balanced scorecard, not a single number:

- **Attendance:** core sessions at or above the January–June 2025 monthly averages (craft 30.5, film 17.0, family 39.7). New strands must add net new attendances, not just move people from one session to another.
- **Reach:** new attendees, unique families, postcodes and transport mode. Target at least 20 new member households by 30 June.
- **Revenue:** ticket, donation and café income recorded by strand; no target because the pack has no price data.
- **Cost per attendance:** reported by strand for the April and June decisions, using the same unit as the attendance record.
- **Qualitative:** would-return, what people came for and what got in the way, collected through a short exit survey at the pilots and exhibition.

**Decision gates**

- **20 February — east hall:** written commissioning confirmed? If yes, install and open on 14 March. If no, west hall fallback at reduced scale.
- **24 April — Friday Nights:** average attendance at least 25, at least half of booked seats taken, at least 20 minibus passengers per event, and at least 40% of attendees from outside the town centre. If met, release the two extension nights; if not, stop and return £1,500.
- **30 June — whole programme:** report against the scorecard and recommend what continues into autumn/winter.

These are proposed thresholds; the board should confirm them before the programme opens.

---

## 5. Delivering within the trust's rules

| Requirement | How the plan meets it |

# Harrowgate Community Trust

## Six-month programme plan: January–June 2026

**Programming budget:** £60,000  
**Period:** 1 January – 30 June 2026  
**Prepared for:** the Board of Trustees

> The £60,000 covers programming only. The east hall repair is a separate capital grant application, and the family fund is separate and capped at £9,000. Neither is included in the £60,000.

---

## 1. The plan in brief

The trust's attendance decline is not confined to evenings. Tuesday craft fell 14% and Thursday film fell 22% in 2025. Saturday family rose 21% year-on-year, but that rise is a step-change from introducing childcare, not continuing growth: once both years had childcare (September–December), family attendance was flat (40.0 in 2024 against 39.2 in 2025). Transport may be part of the story, but it cannot explain the fall in morning sessions. The plan therefore keeps the core programme running as a control and adds four bounded pieces of new work, each aimed at a different explanation for the decline.

| Strand | What happens | Explanation tested |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Core programme (control)** | Tuesday craft, Thursday film and Saturday family workshop continue | Is the decline general, or specific to one session? |
| **Family and childcare** | Weekly Saturday workshop with free childcare, funded by the family fund | Caring responsibilities; family demand |
| **Friday Nights** | Eight evening events with a hired minibus, free entry and measured attendance | Transport; evening demand |
| **Sunday Sessions** | Six low-cost afternoon sessions | Changed habits and time preference; there is no local evidence |
| **East hall** | A spring exhibition and a May–June community season, gated on HVAC commissioning | Programming quality and scale; better use of the building |

Two gates keep the board in control: **20 February** (east hall) and **24 April** (Friday Nights). A final evaluation on **30 June** recommends what should continue.

---

## 2. Month-by-month schedule

### January 2026 — baseline and first tests

- **Core:** Tuesday craft group on 6, 13, 20 and 27 January, 10:00–12:00, workshop room. Thursday film club on 8, 15, 22 and 29 January, 19:00–21:00, west hall. Saturday family workshop on 3, 10, 17, 24 and 31 January, 10:00–12:00, west hall, with free childcare 10:00–14:00 from the family fund.
- **Friday Nights:** #1 on Friday 16 January and #2 on Friday 30 January, 19:00–21:30, west hall and café. Minibus from the market square at 18:15, returning at 21:45. Free entry, donations. #1 is a local history talk; #2 is a film and discussion.
- **Sunday Sessions:** #1 on Sunday 25 January, 14:00–16:00, west hall: a winter talk and simple making session.
- **Evidence:** by Friday 9 January, compile the 2025 monthly baseline; brief staff and volunteers on counting, postcodes and transport mode; open booking for January and February. The booking sheet records seats reserved, seats taken, minibus passengers and how people got home.
- **East hall:** no activity. Confirm in writing with the building officer and the council the grant approval, repair date and commissioning test. Do not book the hall until commissioning is confirmed.
- **Marketing:** launch the season; £600 on local print, social media and targeted distribution to the four estates and family networks.

### February 2026 — confirm the east hall; keep the tests running

- **Core:** craft on 3, 10 and 24 February (no session on 17 February, half-term); film on 5, 12, 19 and 26 February; family workshop on 7, 14, 21 and 28 February with childcare.
- **Friday Nights:** #3 on Friday 13 February (music and spoken word) and #4 on Friday 27 February (film and discussion), with the minibus.
- **Sunday Sessions:** #2 on Sunday 22 February, 14:00–16:00.
- **East hall gate — Friday 20 February:** if commissioning is confirmed for 1 March, release the spring exhibition installation (9–13 March) and opening (14 March). If commissioning is not confirmed, move the exhibition to the west hall and workshop room at reduced scale, keep the dates, and use the contingency for temporary display. No sensitive material is stored in the east hall or the basement in either case.
- **Marketing:** spring exhibition call-out to local makers and community groups; half-term family promotion.

### March 2026 — the east hall opens

- **Core:** craft on 3, 10, 17, 24 and 31 March; film on 5, 12, 19 and 26 March; family workshop on 7, 14, 21 and 28 March with childcare.
- **East hall:** install Monday 9–Friday 13 March. “Made in Harrowgate” opens on Saturday 14 March, 18:00–20:00, and runs to Sunday 12 April. Eight artist-led workshops run at weekends, in the workshop room and east hall. The opening event has two staff.
- **Friday Nights:** #5 on Friday 13 March and #6 on Friday 27 March, with the minibus.
- **Sunday Sessions:** #3 on Sunday 22 March.
- **Marketing:** exhibition and Easter campaign.
- **If the gate failed:** the exhibition is in the west hall at 60 capacity, the workshop programme is capped accordingly, and the opening event moves to the café.

### April 2026 — Easter, and the Friday decision

- **Core:** craft on 7, 14, 21 and 28 April; film on 9, 23 and 30 April (fortnightly, plus an extra screening); family workshop on 4, 11, 18 and 25 April with childcare.
- **Easter family day:** Saturday 4 April, 10:00–14:00, east hall (or west hall if the gate failed). Two artist-led sessions, materials for 80 participants, café open. It combines with the regular Saturday workshop, so the usual childcare applies.
- **Spring exhibition:** closes Sunday 12 April.
- **Friday Nights:** #7 on Friday 10 April and #8 on Friday 24 April, with the minibus.
- **Sunday Sessions:** #4 on Sunday 19 April.
- **Friday gate — Friday 24 April:** review the eight events against the 2023 pilot: average attendance, booking-to-attendance conversion, minibus passengers, postcodes, and whether people say they would return. If the thresholds are met, release #9 (15 May) and #10 (12 June). If not, cancel them and return the £1,500 to the board.
- **Marketing:** Easter and May campaign.

### May 2026 — second east hall season

- **Core:** craft on 5, 12 and 19 May (no session on 26 May, half-term); film on 7 and 21 May; family workshop on 2, 9, 16, 23 and 30 May with childcare.
- **East hall:** “Harrowgate Open” community season installs 18–22 May, opens Saturday 23 May and runs to Sunday 21 June. Six workshops with schools and community groups; family-friendly.
- **Friday Nights:** #9 on Friday 15 May, only if the April gate was met.
- **Sunday Sessions:** #5 on Sunday 17 May.
- **Budget review:** mid-May, compare actuals with the budget and confirm the contingency position before the summer showcase.
- **Marketing:** bank holiday and half-term campaign.

### June 2026 — summer showcase and evaluation

- **Core:** craft on 2, 9, 16, 23 and 30 June; film on 4, 18 and 25 June; family workshop on 6, 13, 20 and 27 June with childcare.
- **East hall:** the season continues. **Summer Showcase** on Saturday 20 June, 12:00–20:00, east hall and café: performances, a makers' market and family activities. Two staff after 18:00; building empty by 21:00.
- **Friday Nights:** #10 on Friday 12 June, only if the gate was met.
- **Sunday Sessions:** #6 on Sunday 14 June.
- **Evaluation:** 22–30 June. Compile attendance, reach, revenue, membership and cost per attendance by strand; report to the board on 30 June with a recommendation for autumn/winter.
- **Marketing:** summer showcase and membership campaign.

---

### Budget notes

- The east hall repair (£18,000) is a capital grant application and is not in this budget.
- Childcare is not in this budget; it is a draw on the separate family fund (see below).
- No earned income is assumed. The pack gives no ticket prices, so ticket, donation and café income will be recorded separately rather than forecast.
- The £1,500 Friday extension is released only if the 24 April gate is met. If it is not, the programme total is £58,500 and the balance returns to the board.
- Contingency covers repair delay and west hall fallback, artist replacement, extra minibus runs and accessibility costs. It is released by the director with the board chair's agreement.

### Family fund memo (outside the £60,000)

| Item | Basis | £ |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Saturday childcare, weekly | 26 × £180 | 4,680 |
| Family fund cap | | 9,000 |
| Remaining if weekly childcare is approved | | 4,320 |

The cap does not prevent weekly childcare: 26 Saturdays at £180 is £4,680, just over half of the £9,000. The real constraint is that the trustees have not committed the fund. The plan asks for a decision at the board's January meeting so that families can be told. If the trustees approve only fortnightly childcare (13 × £180 = £2,340), the Saturday workshop still runs every week; only the childcare is reduced. The £60,000 programme does not backfill childcare without a separate board decision.

---

## 4. Rationale: evidence and uncertainty

### 4.1 What I relied on

The attendance record (`attendance-2024-2025.csv`) is the strongest evidence because it records behaviour rather than opinion. Comparing 2025 with 2024:

- Tuesday craft: average 33.9 → 29.2 (−14%).
- Thursday film: 20.7 → 16.2 (−22%).
- Saturday family: 31.2 → 37.8 (+21%), but the gain is concentrated in January–August 2025, when 2024 had no childcare. In September–December, when both years had childcare, the averages are 40.0 (2024) and 39.2 (2025). The family session has the strongest attendance level, but it is not on a continuing growth curve.

The decline is therefore broad-based across the core programme: craft and film are down, and the family gain is a step-up that has flattened. That matters. Transport may depress evening attendance, but it cannot by itself explain the fall in Tuesday-morning craft or Saturday-morning family workshops. The plan does not treat transport as the single cause.

The 2025 member survey (`member-survey-2025.md`) puts transport first (61%), but the volunteer's method note is explicit that the evening-transport question was hypothetical: “we asked people to imagine a bus”, with no price test and no behaviour test. 35% said they would not attend even with transport. I treat the survey as a reason to test transport, not as proof of demand. Childcare is cited by 27%, and 81% of those are members with children under 12; that is consistent with the family strand, but it is still a stated preference.

The staff interviews (`staff-interviews.md`) provide two useful facts and one opinion. The facts: the 2023 pilot had no minibus because driver funding fell through, and attendance fell 37 → 23 → 19 while bookings fell 60 → 48. The opinion: “people liked the films; the problem was getting home.” The opinion is plausible, but the pilot is not a clean test of evening demand. It never offered transport, and the first-night booking-to-attendance conversion was only 62%, so something else may also have been happening. The right response is a small, instrumented retest with transport, not a permanent ban or a full-scale commitment.

The prior interventions (`prior-interventions.md`) support a portfolio rather than a single bet. The 2024 childcare pilot is the best positive signal (average 27 → 42), but it is a before/after comparison confounded by seasonality, novelty and the fact that 2024 was already a declining year. The 2022 outreach van had no written evaluation. The 2024 website migration raised traffic 12% but did not change attendance, which suggests that marketing and website work alone will not reverse the decline. The 2023 film pilot is a negative signal about evening events without transport, not a verdict on evening events with transport.

The building and money facts (`constraints.md`, `spaces-and-costs.md`) set the boundaries. The east hall HVAC failed in January 2025; the £18,000 repair is a separate capital grant, expected in late February 2026 and usable from 1 March only if approved and commissioned. The 2019 “climate-controlled” description is stale and is not relied on. The family fund is separate and capped at £9,000; 26 Saturdays × £180 = £4,680, so weekly childcare fits the cap with £4,320 to spare. The binding constraint is trustee discretion, not the cap, so the plan asks for a decision but does not make the family workshop depend on it.

### 4.2 Earlier notes I have corrected

| Earlier note | How I treat it |
| --- | --- |
| “East hall is climate-controlled” (2019 survey, carried forward) | Not relied on. The HVAC failed in January 2025; the hall is used only after written commissioning. |
| “2023 evening pilot failed” | A negative signal, not a settled verdict. The pilot had no transport; bookings were 60 and 48 against attendance of 37, 23 and 19. |
| “Members want evening events” | An overread of a stated preference. 44% said yes, 21% maybe and 35% no; the method note says the question was hypothetical. |
| “Saturday childcare raised attendance” | Promising but not proven. The 27 → 42 step-up is real, but the 2025 gain flattens once both years have childcare. |

The 2023 note's own condition — do not repeat an evening series without transport — is met: every Friday Night has a minibus and two staff. That is the difference between repeating the pilot and testing the question it left open.

### 4.3 What I am uncertain about

- **The cause of the decline.** It is probably multiple. The plan is designed to discriminate between explanations, not to prove one. If the Friday pilot succeeds and Sunday fails, transport and evening access look more important. If both fail while the east hall exhibition draws new people, programming and scale look more important. If everything stays flat, changed habits are the better explanation.
- **Whether transport is the binding constraint.** The survey is stated preference, and the 2023 pilot lacked transport. The Friday test gives a behavioural answer, but eight events is a small sample and winter weather may depress turnout.
- **Whether childcare is causal.** The step-up could be a one-off level shift, seasonality or novelty. The plan continues it because it is affordable and consistent with the evidence, but it measures unique families and repeat attendance rather than assuming the effect.
- **East hall timing.** The repair and commissioning are outside the trust's control. The 20 February gate and the west hall fallback protect the programme, but if commissioning slips beyond June, the board's east hall requirement cannot be met in this period.
- **Sunday demand.** There is no local evidence, and the survey ranks Sunday afternoon last (12%). The pilot is deliberately small; it is a probe, not a core bet.
- **The attendance unit in the CSV.** The file does not say whether the figures are monthly totals or per-session averages. The materials assumptions use 10–12 participants per session and should be checked against the register. If the figures are per-session, materials will cost more and the contingency or the board will need to adjust.
- **Income.** The pack contains no ticket price or earned-income data, so the plan does not assume income. Revenue will be tracked, not targeted.
- **Staff capacity.** The plan budgets bought-in evening cover, but 20 film nights plus 10 Friday Nights is a heavy evening roster. If cover cannot be recruited, the film club should move to fortnightly and the savings held.

### 4.4 How success will be judged

A balanced scorecard, not a single number:

- **Attendance:** core sessions at or above the January–June 2025 monthly averages (craft 30.5, film 17.0, family 39.7). New strands must add net new attendances, not just move people from one session to another.
- **Reach:** new attendees, unique families, postcodes and transport mode. Target at least 20 new member households by 30 June.
- **Revenue:** ticket, donation and café income recorded by strand; no target because the pack has no price data.
- **Cost per attendance:** reported by strand for the April and June decisions, using the same unit as the attendance record.
- **Qualitative:** would-return, what people came for and what got in the way, collected through a short exit survey at the pilots and exhibition.

**Decision gates**

- **20 February — east hall:** written commissioning confirmed? If yes, install and open on 14 March. If no, west hall fallback at reduced scale.
- **24 April — Friday Nights:** average attendance at least 25, at least half of booked seats taken, at least 20 minibus passengers per event, and at least 40% of attendees from outside the town centre. If met, release the two extension nights; if not, stop and return £1,500.
- **30 June — whole programme:** report against the scorecard and recommend what continues into autumn/winter.

These are proposed thresholds; the board should confirm them before the programme opens.

---

## 5. Delivering within the trust's rules

| Requirement | How the plan meets it |
| --- | --- |
| **Staffing** | Two staff at every evening event; volunteers are never alone after 18:00. Evening cover is bought in at £220 per event and is included in the film and Friday budgets. |
| **Childcare** | Two qualified workers per Saturday session, four hours, £180, paid by the family fund. No childcare is charged to the £60,000. |
| **Licensing** | Film screenings use the £120 film licence. Any live music is programmed only if it is covered by the trust's existing premises licence; otherwise the Friday programme uses talks, spoken word and film. |
| **Times** | Film ends at 21:00; Friday Nights end at 21:30; the building is empty by 22:15. The summer showcase ends at 20:00. No event runs past 23:00. |
| **Rooms** | Craft in the workshop room (24); film and family in the west hall (60); east hall (120 seated / 180 standing) only after commissioning. The basement is not used for sensitive material. |
| **Family fund** | Separate from the £60,000. Weekly childcare would use £4,680 of the £9,000 cap; the workshop continues if the fund is not released. |
| **Single funder** | No core session depends on a single external funder. The family fund supports childcare only; the core programme is funded by the £60,000. |

---

# Harrowgate Community Trust

## Six-month programme plan: January–June 2026

**Programming budget:** £60,000  
**Period:** 1 January – 30 June 2026  
**Prepared for:** the Board of Trustees

> The £60,000 covers programming only. The east hall repair is a separate capital grant application, and the family fund is separate and capped at £9,000. Neither is included in the £60,000.

---

## 1. The plan in brief

The trust's attendance decline is not confined to evenings. Tuesday craft fell 14% and Thursday film fell 22% in 2025. Saturday family rose 21% year-on-year, but that rise coincides with the introduction of childcare and is not continuing growth: once both years had childcare (September–December), family attendance was flat (40.0 in 2024 against 39.2 in 2025). Transport may be part of the story, but it cannot explain the fall in Tuesday-morning craft or the flattening of Saturday family attendance. The plan therefore keeps the core programme running as a baseline and adds four bounded pieces of work, each aimed at a different explanation for the decline.

| Strand | What happens | Explanation tested |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Core programme (baseline)** | Tuesday craft, Thursday film and Saturday family workshop continue | Is the decline general, or specific to one session? |
| **Family and childcare** | Weekly Saturday workshop (programming budget) with free childcare (family fund) | Caring responsibilities; family demand |
| **Friday Nights** | Eight evening events with a hired minibus, free entry and measured attendance | Transport; evening demand |
| **Sunday Sessions** | Six low-cost afternoon talk-and-making sessions | Changed habits and time preference; there is no local evidence |
| **East hall** | A spring exhibition and a May–June community season, gated on HVAC commissioning | Programming quality and scale; better use of the building |

The strands map onto the board's three explanations and the survey's caring-responsibility barrier: Friday Nights tests transport; the family strand tests caring and family demand; Sunday Sessions test time and habit; the east hall season tests programming quality and scale. The core programme is the baseline against which the new work is judged.

Two gates keep the board in control: **20 February** (east hall) and **27 April** (Friday Nights). A final evaluation on **30 June** recommends what should continue.

---

## 2. Month-by-month schedule

### January 2026 — baseline and first tests

- **Core:** Tuesday craft group on 6, 13, 20 and 27 January, 10:00–12:00, workshop room. Thursday film club on 8, 15, 22 and 29 January, 19:00–21:00, west hall. Saturday family workshop on 3, 10, 17, 24 and 31 January, 10:00–12:00, west hall, with free childcare 10:00–14:00 from the family fund.
- **Friday Nights:** #1 on Friday 16 January and #2 on Friday 30 January, 19:00–21:30, west hall and café. Minibus from the market square at 18:15 (before the last scheduled service at 18:40), returning at 21:45. Free entry, so the test isolates transport from price; donations welcome. #1 is a local history talk; #2 is a film and discussion.
- **Sunday Sessions:** #1 on Sunday 25 January, 14:00–16:00, west hall: a winter talk and simple making session. Free entry, donations.
- **Evidence:** by Friday 9 January, compile the 2025 monthly baseline; brief staff and volunteers on counting, postcodes and transport mode; open booking for January and February. The booking sheet records seats reserved, seats taken, minibus passengers and how people got home.
- **East hall:** no activity. Confirm in writing with the building officer and the council the grant approval, repair date and commissioning test. Do not book the hall until commissioning is confirmed.
- **Marketing:** launch the season; within the £600 monthly budget, local print, social media and targeted distribution to the four estates and family networks.

### February 2026 — confirm the east hall; keep the tests running

- **Core:** craft on 3, 10 and 24 February (no session on 17 February, half-term); film on 5, 12, 19 and 26 February; family workshop on 7, 14, 21 and 28 February with childcare.
- **Friday Nights:** #3 on Friday 13 February (music and spoken word) and #4 on Friday 27 February (film and discussion), with the minibus.
- **Sunday Sessions:** #2 on Sunday 22 February, 14:00–16:00.
- **East hall gate — Friday 20 February:** if commissioning is confirmed for 1 March, release the spring exhibition installation (9–13 March) and opening (14 March). If commissioning is not confirmed, move the exhibition to the west hall and workshop room at reduced scale, keep the dates, and use the contingency for temporary display. No sensitive material is stored in the east hall before commissioning, or in the basement at any point.
- **Marketing:** spring exhibition call-out to local makers and community groups; half-term family promotion.

### March 2026 — the east hall opens

- **Core:** craft on 3, 10, 17, 24 and 31 March; film on 5, 12, 19 and 26 March; family workshop on 7, 14, 21 and 28 March with childcare.
- **East hall:** install Monday 9–Friday 13 March. “Made in Harrowgate” opens on Saturday 14 March, 18:00–20:00, and runs to Sunday 12 April. Eight artist-led workshops run at weekends, in the workshop room and east hall. The opening event has two staff.
- **Friday Nights:** #5 on Friday 13 March and #6 on Friday 27 March, with the minibus.
- **Sunday Sessions:** #3 on Sunday 22 March.
- **Marketing:** exhibition and Easter campaign.
- **If the gate failed:** the exhibition is in the west hall at 60 capacity, the workshop programme is capped accordingly, and the opening event moves to the café.

### April 2026 — Easter, and the Friday decision

- **Core:** craft on 7, 14, 21 and 28 April; film on 9 and 23 April, plus an extra screening on 30 April; family workshop on 4, 11, 18 and 25 April with childcare.
- **Easter family day:** Saturday 4 April, 10:00–14:00, east hall (or west hall if the gate failed). Two artist-led sessions; materials for up to 80 participants in the east hall, capped at 60 in the west hall; café open. It combines with the regular Saturday workshop, so the usual childcare applies.
- **Spring exhibition:** closes Sunday 12 April.
- **Friday Nights:** #7 on Friday 10 April and #8 on Friday 24 April, with the minibus.
- **Sunday Sessions:** #4 on Sunday 19 April.
- **Friday gate — Monday 27 April:** review the eight events against the 2023 pilot: average attendance, booking-to-attendance conversion, minibus passengers, postcodes, and whether people say they would return. The extra days allow the 24 April event data to be entered. If the thresholds are met, release #9 (15 May) and #10 (12 June). If not, cancel them and return the £1,500 to the board.
- **Marketing:** Easter and May campaign.

### May 2026 — second east hall season

## 4. Rationale: evidence and uncertainty

### 4.1 What I relied on

The attendance record (`attendance-2024-2025.csv`) is the strongest evidence because it records behaviour rather than opinion. Comparing 2025 with 2024:

- Tuesday craft: average 33.9 → 29.2 (−14%).
- Thursday film: 20.7 → 16.2 (−22%).
- Saturday family: 31.2 → 37.8 (+21%), but the gain is concentrated in January–August 2025, when 2024 had no childcare. In September–December, when both years had childcare, the averages are 40.0 (2024) and 39.2 (2025). The family session has the strongest attendance level, but it is not on a continuing growth curve.

The decline is therefore broad-based across the core programme: craft and film are down, and the family gain is a step-up that has flattened. That matters. Transport may depress evening attendance, but it cannot by itself explain the fall in Tuesday-morning craft or the flattening of Saturday-morning family attendance. The plan does not treat transport as the single cause. The staff description of the craft group as “loyal but ageing” is consistent with the slow decline; the plan keeps it as a core service but does not rely on it for growth.

The 2025 member survey (`member-survey-2025.md`) puts transport first (61%), but the volunteer's method note is explicit that the evening-transport question was hypothetical: “we asked people to imagine a bus”, with no price test and no behaviour test. 35% said they would not attend even with transport. I treat the survey as a reason to test transport, not as proof of demand. Childcare is cited by 27%, and 81% of those are members with children under 12; that is consistent with the family strand, but it is still a stated preference.

The staff interviews (`staff-interviews.md`) provide two useful factual claims and one opinion. The account says the 2023 pilot had no minibus because driver funding fell through; the booking records show attendance fell 37 → 23 → 19 while bookings fell 60 → 48. The opinion is: “people liked the films; the problem was getting home.” The opinion is plausible, but the pilot is not a clean test of evening demand. It never offered transport, and the first-night booking-to-attendance conversion was only 62%, so something else may also have been happening. The right response is a small, instrumented retest with transport, not a permanent ban or a full-scale commitment.

The prior interventions (`prior-interventions.md`) support a portfolio rather than a single bet. The 2024 childcare pilot is the best positive signal (about 27 → 40 in the attendance record; the prior review rounds this to 42), but it is a before/after comparison confounded by seasonality, novelty and the fact that 2024 was already a declining year. Staff also report that families stayed for the café and some moved to the Tuesday craft group; that spillover is worth measuring, not assuming. The 2022 outreach van had no written evaluation. The 2024 website migration raised traffic 12%, but there is no evidence that it changed attendance, which suggests that marketing and website work alone will not reverse the decline. The 2023 film pilot is a negative signal about evening events without transport, not a verdict on evening events with transport.

The building and money facts (`constraints.md`, `spaces-and-costs.md`) set the boundaries. The east hall HVAC failed in January 2025; the £18,000 repair is a separate capital grant, expected in late February 2026 and usable from 1 March only if approved and commissioned. The 2019 “climate-controlled” description is stale and is not relied on. The family fund is separate and capped at £9,000; 26 Saturdays × £180 = £4,680, so weekly childcare fits the cap with £4,320 to spare. On these figures, the binding constraint is trustee discretion, not the cap, so the plan asks for a decision but does not make the family workshop depend on it.

### 4.2 Earlier notes I have corrected

| Earlier note | How I treat it |
| --- | --- |
| “East hall is climate-controlled” (2019 survey, carried forward) | Not relied on. The HVAC failed in January 2025; the hall is used only after written commissioning. |
| “2023 evening pilot failed” | A negative signal, not a settled verdict. The pilot had no transport; bookings were 60 and 48 against attendance of 37, 23 and 19. |
| “Members want evening events” | An overread of a stated preference. 44% said yes, 21% maybe and 35% no; the method note says the question was hypothetical. |
| “Saturday childcare raised attendance” | Promising but not proven. The step-up is visible in the record, but the 2025 gain flattens once both years have childcare. |

The 2023 note's own condition — do not repeat an evening series without transport — is met: every Friday Night has a minibus and two staff. That is the difference between repeating the pilot and testing the question it left open.

### 4.3 What I am uncertain about

- **The cause of the decline.** It is probably multiple. The plan is designed to discriminate between explanations, not to prove one. If the Friday pilot succeeds and Sunday fails, transport and evening access look more important. If both fail while the east hall exhibition draws new people, programming and scale look more important. If everything stays flat, changed habits are the better explanation.
- **Whether transport is the binding constraint.** The survey is stated preference, and the 2023 pilot lacked transport. The Friday test gives a behavioural answer, but eight events is a small sample and winter weather may depress turnout.
- **Whether childcare is causal.** The step-up could be a one-off level shift, seasonality or novelty. The plan continues it because it is affordable and consistent with the evidence, but it measures unique families and repeat attendance rather than assuming the effect.
- **East hall timing.** The repair and commissioning are outside the trust's control. The 20 February gate and the west hall fallback protect the programme, but if commissioning slips beyond June, the board's east hall requirement cannot be met in this period.
- **Sunday demand.** There is no local evidence, and the survey ranks Sunday afternoon last (12%). The pilot is deliberately small; it is a probe, not a core bet.
- **The attendance unit in the CSV.** The file does not say whether the figures are monthly totals or per-session averages. The materials assumptions use 10–12 participants per session and should be checked against the register. If the figures are per-session, materials will cost more and the craft group would need the west hall; the contingency or the board will need to adjust.
- **Income.** The pack contains no ticket price or earned-income data, so the plan does not assume income. Revenue will be tracked, not targeted.
- **Staff capacity.** The plan budgets bought-in evening cover, but 20 film screenings plus 10 Friday Nights is a heavy evening roster. If cover cannot be recruited, the film club should move to fortnightly and the savings held.

### 4.4 How success will be judged

A balanced scorecard, not a single number:

- **Attendance:** core sessions at or above the January–June 2025 monthly averages (craft 30.5, film 17.0, family 39.7). New strands must add net new attendances, not just move people from one session to another.
- **Reach:** new attendees, unique families, postcodes and transport mode. Target at least 20 new member households by 30 June.
- **Revenue:** ticket, donation and café income recorded by strand; no target because the pack has no price data.
- **Cost per attendance:** reported by strand for the April and June decisions, using the same unit as the attendance record.
- **Qualitative:** would-return, what people came for and what got in the way, collected through a short exit survey at the pilots and exhibition.

**Decision gates**

- **20 February — east hall:** written commissioning confirmed? If yes, install and open on 14 March. If no, west hall fallback at reduced scale.
- **27 April — Friday Nights:** average attendance at least 25, at least 40% of booked seats taken, at least 12 minibus passengers per event (a 16-seat minibus at least three-quarters full), and at least 40% of attendees from outside the town centre. If met, release the two extension nights; if not, stop and return £1,500.
- **30 June — whole programme:** report against the scorecard and recommend what continues into autumn/winter.

These are proposed thresholds; the board should confirm them before the programme opens.
